title: The Bloop: The Ocean Sound Nobody Could Explain

scenes.narration: That sound was recorded in the Pacific Ocean in 1997.

scenes.narration: And some believed the U.S. Navy knew more than it was saying.

camera.position: next to a hydrophone mooring cable

scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.lighting: Near-black; submarine hull catches a faint blue sheen
scenes.animation: Hull passes left to right over 4 s.
scenes.sound_notes: Muffled machinery hum, no sonar pings.

scenes.narration: Scientists gave it a name that sounds almost like a joke. The Bloop.
scenes.visual_intent: Title reveal: the word 'The Bloop' forms out of the real waveform.
scenes.animation: Waveform line contracts into the title lettering.
scenes.sound_notes: A short excerpt of the real clip under the title.

scenes.narration: Tonight we follow every one of those theories, as far as they go. And at the end, we will show you what the people who recorded the sound actually found.
scenes.visual_intent: Promise to the viewer, then the channel card.
scenes.animation: Ident card: STRANGER HORIZONS — Explore Beyond What We Know.
scenes.sound_notes: Ident tone (owner-approved music from YouTube Audio Library).

scenes.narration: Light fades quickly in the sea. Go deep enough, and the ocean is completely dark. But sound behaves differently.
scenes.visual_intent: Descent from the bright surface into darkness.
scenes.environment: Open ocean from surface to 300 m
scenes.lighting: Sun from above fading with depth
scenes.animation: Light shafts thin out as the camera sinks.
scenes.sound_notes: Surface wash fading to deep hum.

scenes.narration: Deep in the ocean there is a layer where sound travels at its slowest, and that layer traps it. Inside it, a low rumble can cross an entire ocean basin.
scenes.visual_intent: Explain the deep sound channel.
scenes.animation: A pulse leaves a source, bends up and down along the channel axis and travels across the frame.
scenes.sound_notes: Soft low pulse sound design (labelled as illustration, not a recording).

scenes.narration: During the Cold War, the U.S. Navy wired parts of the deep sea with microphones to hunt submarines. When the Cold War ended, scientists were allowed to listen too, and they heard volcanoes erupting on the seafloor.
scenes.visual_intent: Cold War listening cables on the seafloor.

camera.position: 1 m above seabed following a cable

scenes.environment: Mid-water seabed (~150 m): sediment, basalt boulders (EP000 set kit)
scenes.lighting: Cold, motivated by distant lamp; mostly dark
scenes.animation: Camera follows a cable to a listening node; a faint glow of a distant eruption on the horizon.

scenes.narration: So NOAA's Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory built listening stations of its own. In May 1996, it moored a line of hydrophones in the eastern equatorial Pacific, to hear earthquakes and eruptions on the seafloor.
scenes.visual_intent: NOAA's own moored hydrophone in the dark.

camera.movement: rise along the mooring cable 10 m

scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.lighting: Faint blue ambient; hydrophone catches rim light
scenes.animation: Cable sways slightly in current; marine snow drifts.

scenes.narration: Then, in the summer of 1997, the hydrophones caught something else.
scenes.visual_intent: Something arrives: the hydrophone in close-up, a faint vibration.
scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.animation: Particles near the hydrophone tremble very slightly.

scenes.narration: A powerful, low sound. NOAA described its pitch as rising rapidly, over about a minute.
scenes.visual_intent: The real evidence: our spectrogram of NOAA's file draws itself while the real audio plays.
scenes.on_screen_label: Spectrogram generated from the NOAA recording (sped up 16×)
scenes.animation: Spectrogram reveals left to right in sync with the audio; the rising sweep is highlighted.

scenes.narration: It came again and again that summer. And it was loud enough to reach several hydrophones more than five thousand kilometres away. The version you heard has been sped up sixteen times, so that human ears can hear it at all.
scenes.visual_intent: Repeated detections and the speed-up: a summer-1997 timeline with repeated ticks, then a '16×' playback-speed badge on the waveform.
scenes.on_screen_label: Spectrogram generated from the NOAA recording (sped up 16×)
scenes.animation: Timeline ticks appear across summer 1997 (illustrative spacing, labelled); waveform speeds up with a 16× badge.

scenes.narration: NOAA's first estimate placed its source in the remote South Pacific, roughly fifty degrees south and one hundred degrees west, far off the coast of southern South America.
scenes.visual_intent: Locate the early estimate: 50°S 100°W.

camera.movement: zoom from Pacific to South Pacific

scenes.animation: Globe rotates; marker drops at 50°S 100°W with coordinates text.

scenes.narration: Earthquakes rumble. Ships hum. This was different. Its pitch changed quickly, the way animal calls do.
scenes.visual_intent: Comparison: an earthquake, a ship and the Bloop as three spectrogram shapes.
scenes.animation: Panels appear one by one; the Bloop's rising line is highlighted.

scenes.narration: In 2002, the scientist leading NOAA's acoustic monitoring work, Christopher Fox, told New Scientist that of all the unexplained sounds his team had collected, this was the one that most resembled an animal.
scenes.visual_intent: Fox's 2002 remark: a recreated, empty acoustics lab (no people), monitors showing the real spectrogram; citation card 'New Scientist, 15 June 2002 (paraphrased)'.
scenes.environment: Generic 1990s acoustics lab, night, no people, no real logos
scenes.lighting: Monitor glow, desk lamp (Ember Amber accent)
scenes.animation: Monitor shows the spectrogram scrolling; citation card fades in.

scenes.narration: But to be heard so far away, the source had to be enormous, or enormously efficient at making sound.
scenes.visual_intent: Distance as a puzzle: a pulse ring spans five thousand kilometres.
scenes.animation: Ring expands from the source to the hydrophones; a ruler reads '> 5,000 km'.

scenes.narration: NOAA's own list of guesses from that time reads like the start of a thriller: secret military exercises, ship engines, fishing-boat winches, giant squid, whales, an unknown creature.
scenes.visual_intent: NOAA's list of guesses as an animated list card.
assets: List card: military exercises, ship engines, fishing-boat winches, giant squid, whales, unknown creature
scenes.animation: Items appear one by one, the last one ('unknown creature') lingers.

scenes.narration: And by NOAA's estimate, around ninety-five percent of the ocean is unexplored. A sound with no source, from a place almost no one has seen. The theories wrote themselves.
scenes.visual_intent: Unknown ocean: camera hangs above an unexplored abyss.

camera.movement: slow push toward a dark trench
camera.position: over the edge of a deep trench

scenes.environment: Abyssal plain falling into a trench
scenes.lighting: Single faint shaft; trench is black
scenes.animation: Marine snow falls into the dark.

scenes.narration: Theory one: the giant. By 2002, news reports were asking whether a giant creature was hiding in the deep, perhaps a giant squid.
scenes.visual_intent: THEORY ONE title card, then the Giant appears.

camera.movement: rise 6 m as the creature rises
camera.position: beside a tiny ROV for scale

scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.lighting: ROV lamps catch the creature's skin; backlit by a shaft
scenes.animation: Creature rises past the ROV, arms uncoiling slowly; mantle pulses; never attacks.
scenes.sound_notes: Deep pressure, water movement; no creature voice.

scenes.narration: The most repeated line was that the Bloop was several times louder than a blue whale, the loudest known animal. If that were true, the reasoning went, whatever made it had to be bigger than anything alive.
scenes.visual_intent: The Giant's scale: its eye slides through the ROV's lamp beam.

camera.movement: lateral track with the creature 5 m

scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.animation: A huge eye slides through the ROV's beam; ROV is dwarfed.

scenes.narration: In 2003, cryptozoologist Loren Coleman wrote that it most likely came from a marine beast. Scientists said "unknown". Many readers heard "monster".
scenes.visual_intent: How the press told it: invented headline cards (no real mastheads) over a dark Giant silhouette.
assets: Invented headline cards (illegible body text, no real mastheads)
scenes.animation: Cards slide in; the word 'MONSTER' sharpens last.

scenes.narration: Theory two: the survivor. Others pictured something older: megalodon, a giant prehistoric shark, still surviving in the deep where no one looks. To believers, the Bloop was its call, finally caught on tape.
scenes.visual_intent: THEORY TWO: the Survivor, megalodon gliding out of the blue-black.

camera.movement: slow push-in, then hold as it banks away
camera.position: mid-water, 30 m ahead of the shark's path

scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.lighting: Shafts from above; shark crosses two shafts
scenes.animation: Shark emerges head-on, banks away, tail sweep; marine snow streams off its fins.

scenes.narration: Theory three: the sleeper. Then there is Cthulhu.
scenes.visual_intent: THEORY THREE title: first glimpse of sunken ruins far below.
scenes.animation: Silt haze; ruins emerge.

scenes.narration: In a horror story published in 1928, H. P. Lovecraft described a sunken city called R'lyeh, where a monstrous god lies dreaming beneath the South Pacific. He even gave its coordinates: forty-seven degrees south, one hundred and twenty-six degrees west.
scenes.visual_intent: THEORY THREE: Lovecraft's 1928 text, the coordinate line legible.
scenes.on_screen_label: From 'The Call of Cthulhu', H. P. Lovecraft, 1928 (public domain)

camera.movement: slow push to the coordinate line

scenes.environment: Aged paper on a dark table (original design, no imitation of a real edition)
scenes.animation: Text blurred except the coordinate line, which sharpens.

scenes.narration: Seventy years later, a mysterious sound rose out of the same ocean. Online, the Bloop was said to come from almost exactly there.
scenes.visual_intent: The Sleeper: camera descends to sunken ruins; an immense dormant figure.
scenes.environment: Abyssal floor, tilted cyclopean monoliths (original design)
assets: CR_Sleeper (original design from the 1928 text only)
scenes.lighting: Cold blue rim; faint bioluminescent cyan in the ruins
scenes.animation: Silt drifts; the figure's folded wings and tentacled head emerge from the dark.

scenes.narration: For some it was a joke. For others it was too perfect to be a coincidence. Hold on to that coordinate. We will come back to it.
scenes.visual_intent: The Sleeper's eye slowly opens; then a map pin 'R'lyeh (fiction)' appears.

camera.position: in front of the figure's closed eye

scenes.animation: Eyelid opens a few millimetres; hold; cut to globe pin.
scenes.sound_notes: Silence for 1 s before the cut.

scenes.narration: Theory four: the Navy knew. Remember who built the ocean's first great listening network. The Navy.
scenes.visual_intent: THEORY FOUR: recreated generic sonar room.
scenes.environment: Generic Cold War-style sonar room (no real insignia or documents)
scenes.animation: Screens show abstract scrolling waterfalls.
scenes.sound_notes: Room hum; no fabricated radio chatter.

scenes.narration: In a NOAA press release from 2001, the agency's own scientist was quoted saying this kind of sound had been reported for decades by Navy sonar operators. Decades. Before anyone had heard of the Bloop.
scenes.visual_intent: The 2001 NOAA release: paraphrase card with source line, over the sonar screens.
scenes.environment: Generic Cold War-style sonar room (no real insignia or documents)
assets: Quote card: paraphrase of NOAA release, 24 Aug 2001
scenes.animation: Screens show abstract scrolling waterfalls; quote card fades in with source line.
scenes.sound_notes: Room hum; no fabricated radio chatter.

scenes.narration: Some retellings go further. They claim the Navy was asked directly, and said it wasn't theirs. To a suspicious mind, that is exactly what you would say about a secret weapon, or a test you could not admit.
scenes.visual_intent: An unmarked submarine passes a lone hydrophone.
scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.animation: Submarine slides past over 6 s; its wake disturbs the particles.

scenes.narration: Theory five: something not from here. In UFO circles, the Bloop became one more "unidentified submerged object". An alien craft, a hidden base on the seafloor, something using the deep ocean the way we use the sky.
scenes.visual_intent: THEORY FIVE: the Visitor rises from a trench.

camera.position: at the lip of a trench

scenes.lighting: Craft's cyan ring is the only light
scenes.animation: Craft rises silently, ring pulses once, scattering particles.
scenes.title_card: THEORY FIVE: SOMETHING NOT FROM HERE

scenes.narration: Theory six: the mermaids. In 2012, a television film presented as a documentary, Mermaids: The Body Found, used the Bloop as part of its evidence for a hidden species of sea people.
scenes.visual_intent: THEORY SIX: stylised TV frame with the note 'Fiction (2012)'.
assets: TV frame graphic (no programme footage or branding)
scenes.animation: Static noise resolves into the 'Fiction (2012)' note.

scenes.narration: It was fiction, with a disclaimer. But enough viewers believed it that the questions reached the U.S. government.
scenes.visual_intent: THEORY SIX: 'Fiction (2012)' TV frame, then distant swimmers at the edge of a lamp beam.
scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
assets: Stylised TV frame with note 'Fiction (2012)' (no programme footage/branding)
scenes.animation: Two figures cross the far edge of the beam and vanish; never close-up.

scenes.narration: And finally: the legend. Online, the Bloop grew a body. It got fan-made creature designs, invented expedition stories, and animated battles against other sea monsters.
scenes.visual_intent: The legend online: invented, illegible forum threads and fan-art style creature sketches.
scenes.animation: Threads scroll; sketches pile up.

scenes.narration: The story itself kept changing as it spread. It was heard only once. It lasted fifteen seconds. Every microphone picked it up. It was never heard again.
scenes.visual_intent: The 'Bloop Beast' of internet legend surfacing in a storm.

camera.movement: aerial pull-back over a storm sea

scenes.lighting: Lightning flashes; creature lit only by flashes
scenes.animation: Phone screens flicker, then the leviathan's back breaks the surface.

scenes.narration: Even today, some articles still call it unsolved.
scenes.visual_intent: Headlines blur together on screen (invented, illegible).
scenes.animation: Cards stack and shuffle.

scenes.narration: A giant. A survivor. A sleeping god.
scenes.visual_intent: Montage line-up: Giant, Survivor, Sleeper, one shot each.
scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.animation: One beat per creature.
scenes.sound_notes: Music hit per cut (no horror stinger).

scenes.narration: A Navy secret. Visitors. Mermaids.
scenes.visual_intent: Montage line-up continued: submarine, craft, swimmers.
scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.animation: One beat per shot.

scenes.narration: Every one of these theories has believers. But only one explanation has evidence. And it was found by the same people who recorded the sound in the first place.
scenes.visual_intent: Turn: all creatures fade; only the lone hydrophone remains in the dark.
scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.animation: Silence; particles settle.
scenes.sound_notes: Music drops out; 1 s of near silence.

scenes.narration: Here is the part of the story most people never hear. Even in 2001, the team suspected an ordinary answer. Christopher Fox said publicly that they suspected ice, off the coast of Antarctica.
scenes.visual_intent: Reveal begins: a research vessel on a grey swell at dusk.
scenes.animation: Ship pitches gently; spray.
scenes.sound_notes: Wind, swell; music shifts to the Investigation theme.

scenes.narration: But suspicion is not proof. Officially, the Bloop's origin had still not been determined. To be sure, the scientists needed to listen much closer to the ice.
scenes.visual_intent: Map turns south; a faint line from the hydrophones toward Antarctica.
scenes.animation: Dotted line grows south; '?' marker.

scenes.narration: So NOAA went south. In December 2005, a team led by geophysicist Robert Dziak put hydrophones into the water off the Antarctic Peninsula, in the Bransfield Strait. Their arrays kept recording there, and in the Scotia Sea, until 2009.
scenes.visual_intent: Antarctic Peninsula: icebergs, grey light; hydrophone lowered over the side.

camera.movement: glide past icebergs toward the vessel

scenes.environment: Antarctic Peninsula / Southern Ocean: grey swell, tabular icebergs, overcast
scenes.animation: Mooring lowered on a winch; splash.

scenes.narration: Once again, they had come to listen for volcanoes and earthquakes. And once again, they heard ice. Thousands of times.
scenes.visual_intent: Under the ice: dozens of crack-flashes along an iceberg keel.

camera.movement: lateral track under an iceberg keel

scenes.lighting: Glow through the ice from above
scenes.animation: Small crack flashes ripple along the keel, many of them.
scenes.sound_notes: Creaks and cracks (sound design, labelled in description).

scenes.narration: Around Antarctica, cracking ice turned out to be one of the most prominent sounds in the sea. Icebergs groan as they run aground and scrape the seafloor. And when they crack and fracture, they release bursts of sound called icequakes.
scenes.visual_intent: Icequake close-up: a crack propagates; an iceberg scrapes the seafloor.
scenes.animation: Crack races through the ice; fragments shear; keel grinds the seabed raising silt.

scenes.narration: In early 2008, the hydrophones followed one iceberg, known as A53a, about sixty kilometres long, as it broke apart near the island of South Georgia.
scenes.visual_intent: A53a: a 60 km iceberg drifting and splitting near South Georgia (map + 3D).
scenes.environment: Scotia Sea map, South Georgia outline
scenes.animation: Iceberg drifts east and splits into pieces.

scenes.narration: Its icequakes left a familiar shape on the screen. Spectrograms very similar to the Bloop. And icequakes like these can be heard on hydrophones more than five thousand kilometres away.
scenes.visual_intent: Side-by-side: the Bloop spectrogram and NOAA's iceberg calving recording.
scenes.on_screen_label: Spectrograms generated from NOAA recordings: Bloop (1997, 16×) · Iceberg calving (2008, 3×)
scenes.animation: Both draw in; shapes highlighted; note that playback speeds differ.
scenes.sound_notes: Short excerpts of both real NOAA files.

scenes.narration: There was one more clue. A sound reaches each hydrophone at a slightly different moment, and those tiny differences reveal the direction it came from.
scenes.visual_intent: How a bearing works: one wavefront reaching three hydrophones at different times.
scenes.animation: Wavefront sweeps across three markers, timing ticks appear; arrow forms.

scenes.narration: When NOAA traced the Bloop's arrival direction, the line did not stop in that empty patch of ocean. It pointed on, toward the edge of Antarctica, somewhere between the Bransfield Strait and the Ross Sea, or perhaps Cape Adare.
scenes.visual_intent: The bearing line sweeps past 50°S 100°W to the Antarctic coast; arc of possible sources.
assets: Arc Bransfield Strait – Ross Sea – Cape Adare
scenes.animation: Line extends; coastline arc highlights.

scenes.script_section: 5. Scientific explanations (the sound of breaking ice)
scenes.narration: So what is an icequake? Large icebergs are not solid, silent blocks. As they drift, collide and ground, they crack and fracture, and each break releases energy into the water as sound.
scenes.visual_intent: Macro: ice under stress, cracks propagating.
scenes.animation: Micro-cracks branch and release bubbles.

scenes.script_section: 5. Scientific explanations (the sound of breaking ice)
scenes.narration: Low-frequency sound loses little energy in the deep sound channel, so a big enough event can carry across an ocean.
scenes.visual_intent: Sound channel again, now from an iceberg to a distant hydrophone.
scenes.animation: Pulse from iceberg travels along the channel to the hydrophone thousands of km away.

scenes.script_section: 5. Scientific explanations (the sound of breaking ice)
scenes.narration: And it isn't rare. In 2012, Robert Dziak said that every year there are tens of thousands of icequakes. Asked about the Bloop directly, he said its frequency and duration were essentially identical to icequakes his team had recorded off Antarctica.
scenes.visual_intent: Scale of icequakes: a counter of icequakes per year over Antarctic coastline.
scenes.animation: Many small flashes around the coast; caption 'tens of thousands each year (Dziak, 2012)'.

scenes.script_section: 5. Scientific explanations (the sound of breaking ice)
scenes.narration: NOAA's laboratory put its conclusion carefully. The sounds recorded in 1997 are consistent with icequakes generated by large icebergs as they crack and fracture.
scenes.visual_intent: NOAA's conclusion as an on-screen quote card.
assets: Quote card (NOAA PMEL wording, U.S. government work)
scenes.animation: Text types on; source line under it.

scenes.script_section: 5. Scientific explanations (the sound of breaking ice)
scenes.narration: Now listen again, slowed back down to its real speed.
scenes.visual_intent: Set-up for the listening moment: the 16× waveform on screen.
scenes.animation: Waveform pulses once.

scenes.script_section: 5. Scientific explanations (the sound of breaking ice)
scenes.visual_intent: The slowed-down truth: the real NOAA clip at 16×, then a 20–30 s excerpt slowed to approximate real time.
scenes.on_screen_label: Approximate real-time playback — our reconstruction from the NOAA recording
scenes.animation: Spectrogram stretches 16× horizontally as the slowed audio plays; frequency axis relabels to real Hz.
scenes.sound_notes: 16× clip, then slowed excerpt; no music.

scenes.script_section: 5. Scientific explanations (the sound of breaking ice)
scenes.narration: Speeding a recording up sixteen times raises every pitch by four full octaves. NOAA's ten-second clip holds almost three minutes of the original recording.
scenes.visual_intent: Pitch and time: a note climbs four octave rungs; a 165 s bar compresses into 10.3 s.
scenes.animation: Ladder and ruler animate.

scenes.script_section: 5. Scientific explanations (the sound of breaking ice)
scenes.narration: Most of the real sound sits so low that, at its true speed, it is barely audible to human ears.
scenes.visual_intent: Hearing threshold: the true-speed sweep (~9–28 Hz, our analysis) drawn against the ~20 Hz lower edge of typical human hearing.
scenes.animation: Note climbs four octave rungs; a 165 s bar compresses to 10.3 s.

scenes.script_section: 5. Scientific explanations (the sound of breaking ice)
scenes.narration: That short, round, strangely living "bloop" was never the voice of anything. It was a side effect of speeding up a deep, slow rumble so that we could hear it.
scenes.visual_intent: The monster dissolves into sound: the Giant's silhouette turns into a waveform, then into ice.
scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.animation: Silhouette breaks into particles that align into the Bloop waveform.

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: So let's go back through every theory.
scenes.visual_intent: The six theory cards return.
scenes.animation: Cards slide in as a grid.

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: The giant. No published measurement shows the Bloop was "several times louder than a blue whale". That line came from how far the sound travelled, not from measuring it.
scenes.visual_intent: The Giant answered (1/3): the creature freezes mid-motion; 'louder than a blue whale' card marked 'no measurement found'.
scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.animation: Creature motion freezes; frost spreads over its skin.

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: For scale, scientists off Antarctica measured blue whale calls at around 189 underwater decibels, and located calling whales up to two hundred kilometres away.
scenes.visual_intent: The Giant answered (2/3): a real-scale blue whale with its measured call range vs the Bloop's detection range.

camera.movement: pull back from 200 km ring to 5,000 km ring

scenes.animation: Small ring for the whale, then the huge Bloop ring.

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: A sound heard more than five thousand kilometres away needed no animal at all, only a very large source of energy, like breaking ice.
scenes.visual_intent: The Giant answered (3/3): the frozen creature cracks and breaks into drifting ice.
scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
assets: Blue whale vs Bloop distance graphic
scenes.animation: Creature cracks and shatters into ice blocks that drift up.

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: The survivor. Megalodon disappears from the fossil record around two and a half million years ago. There is no evidence that it survives.
scenes.visual_intent: The Survivor answered: megalodon turns to ice; fossil-timeline graphic.
scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
assets: Timeline graphic: ~23 to ~2.6 million years ago
scenes.animation: Shark freezes and fractures.

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: The sleeper. Remember that coordinate. The Bloop's first estimated position was nearly two thousand kilometres from Lovecraft's fictional city. On a world map that looks close. In the ocean, it is not. And NOAA's later direction pointed even farther away, toward Antarctica.
scenes.visual_intent: The Sleeper answered: map with 'R'lyeh (fiction)' and the Bloop's early estimate; measured line ≈ 1,980 km; bearing to Antarctica.

camera.movement: pull back to show both pins and Antarctica

scenes.animation: Ruler draws between pins; then the bearing line sweeps to Antarctica; the Sleeper shot (inset) turns to ice.

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: The Navy. That 2001 quote is real, but nothing else we found supports decades of Navy reports of this sound, and we found no primary source for the story that the Navy was asked and denied it.
scenes.visual_intent: The Navy answered (1/2): the 2001 quote card gets an 'UNVERIFIED' stamp.
scenes.animation: Stamp lands.

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: Fox himself did not believe the sound was man-made, and there is no evidence that it was.
scenes.visual_intent: The Navy answered (2/2): the unmarked submarine dissolves into particles beside the hydrophone.

scenes.narration: The visitors. There is no evidence of any craft.

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: The mermaids. After that broadcast, NOAA issued a public statement: no evidence of aquatic humanoids has ever been found.
scenes.visual_intent: The Mermaids answered: NOAA's statement as a quote card; swimmers fade.

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: The legend. NOAA's own record says the sound was recorded repeatedly, rose over about a minute, and was heard on multiple sensors. And that particular event was never heard again, but sounds just like it are recorded every year.
scenes.visual_intent: The Legend answered: myth vs record table; the Bloop Beast freezes and sinks as ice.
scenes.animation: Myth lines strike through one by one; NOAA facts appear.

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: Now, the honest part. The ice explanation has limits too. No one saw the event. The iceberg was never identified.
scenes.visual_intent: The honest part (1/3): an iceberg at dusk; 'No witness. Iceberg unknown.'

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: We found no scientific paper that analyses the 1997 recording itself; the conclusion lives on NOAA's web pages and in interviews.
scenes.visual_intent: The honest part (2/3): stack of papers and web pages; none analyses the 1997 recording itself.
scenes.environment: Document stack graphic (titles of real cited papers, no fake documents)
assets: Citation cards: Fox 2001, Dziak 2013, Dziak 2015, NOAA PMEL page
scenes.animation: Cards fan out; a missing slot 'paper on the 1997 Bloop — not found'.

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: NOAA says the sound was recorded in summer. On an American agency's page, that most likely means the northern summer, which is winter in Antarctica, when icequakes there are less frequent. Less frequent, not absent.
scenes.visual_intent: The honest part (3/3, season): calendar of 1997 showing northern summer = austral winter, with icequake seasonality.
assets: Season ring: northern vs southern seasons
scenes.animation: Ring rotates to June–August; curve dips but stays above zero.

scenes.script_section: 6. What the evidence actually tells us (investigation of every theory)
scenes.narration: And even NOAA's own pages disagree about when the case was closed: 2005, 2008, or 2012.
scenes.visual_intent: The honest part: three different 'solved' dates side by side.

camera.position: sea level, 200 m from the berg

assets: Open-questions card (no witness, iceberg unknown, no paper on 1997 signal, austral winter, dates differ)
scenes.animation: Three date cards: 2005 (NOAA NOS), 2008 (PMEL data), 2012 (WIRED UK interview).

scenes.narration: Here is our verdict. The Bloop was almost certainly not a creature, a weapon or a visitor. The best-supported explanation, from NOAA's own scientists, is an Antarctic icequake: a giant iceberg cracking apart, its sound carried thousands of kilometres by the ocean's deep sound channel.
scenes.visual_intent: Verdict: a vast tabular iceberg at dusk; camera descends below the waterline into the deep.
scenes.animation: Camera breaks the surface; the berg's dark mass disappears into the deep; one crack flash.
scenes.sound_notes: Surface to underwater transition; one deep crack.

scenes.narration: That conclusion is backed by the sound itself, by its direction, and by everything heard near Antarctica since. But it was never witnessed, and it never will be.
scenes.visual_intent: Verdict card.
assets: VERDICT — Antarctic icequake: strongly supported, not directly observed
scenes.animation: Card holds 3 s after the line.

scenes.narration: Maybe that is the real lesson of the Bloop. The mystery was never about a monster. It was about how little we had been listening.
scenes.visual_intent: Reflection: the lone hydrophone in the dark, the ROV passing far off.
scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.animation: Particles drift; ROV lamps far away.

scenes.narration: NOAA's hydrophones still listen to the ocean, and its scientists have always expected that some of what they hear will remain a mystery.
scenes.visual_intent: NOAA still listening: the hydrophone in the dark, cable rising.
scenes.environment: Deep open ocean, blue-black water, drifting marine snow
scenes.animation: Particles drift.

scenes.narration: The question is no longer what made the Bloop. It is what else the ocean is telling us, that we haven't learned to hear.
scenes.visual_intent: Closing: camera rises toward a faint surface; hydrophone silhouette in foreground.
